description: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars
details:
What it does

Beyond the Void is a 3D storytelling website about the machines NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. You scroll through 13 chapters, flying from Earth to the Moon and then to Mars. Along the way you meet seven machines: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Viking 1, Sojourner, Opportunity and Ingenuity. After the story, you can explore each world freely. You spin the planet, click a glowing marker and see each machine where it really landed.

Each machine has:

a story written by our team

a short narrated video

NASA’s own 3D model

a slider that compares the landing photo with today’s view from orbit (LRO and HiRISE)

a to-scale drawing next to a person

a one-question quiz

links to NASA sources

A timeline from 1967 to 2021 shows the machines arriving year by year. You can also share a link that opens straight to one machine.

Benefits and impact

Most people know about the launches, but not about the hardware that stayed behind. Some of it still works: the laser mirror next to Eagle is still used today. Some of it helped people later: Apollo 12’s astronauts visited Surveyor 3 and took parts of it home. We want students and the public to see these machines as historical sites, not junk. We also want them to see how orbiters still “visit” them today. The site is free, runs in any browser, works on phones and needs no install.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with three.js for the 3D scenes

React and Remotion for the videos

Python with edge-tts for the AI narration voice

Puppeteer for screenshots and testing

Git and GitHub Pages for hosting

NASA data: NASA 3D Resources models, LRO and HiRISE images, NSSDCA and JPL mission pages

We used AI (Claude) to help write code and check facts, and an AI voice for the narration. All of this is disclosed on the site, in the videos and in SI_LOG.md.

Creativity

Instead of a list of facts, the project tells one continuous story through a moving camera. Its most direct feature is the “then and now” slider: one landing site, two photos taken decades apart, one of them from orbit.

What was assessed

Precision: Each fact was cross-checked from sources by NASA, where each machine was connected to it.

Accessibility: Readable text, keyboard functionality, mobile-friendly design.

Rapid loading.

Transparency in scaling: The website states that size and distance in it are not to scale.

Proper citation of each picture and model.

Transparency in the use of AI tools.
